thread.title: White House Plans to Quarantine Potential Ebola‑Exposed Americans in Kenya
thread.title_full: White House Plans to Quarantine Potential Ebola‑Exposed Americans in Kenya

author: DailyMail
title: White House Plans to Quarantine Potential Ebola‑Exposed Americans in Kenya
text:
U.S. officials are coordinating with Kenya to set up a field hospital for asymptomatic Americans who may have been exposed to Ebola, aiming to keep the virus out of the United States as the outbreak spreads in the DRC and Uganda.
The White House has confirmed that Americans who might have been exposed to the Ebola virus could be placed under quarantine in Kenya rather than being returned to the United States .
In a statement to the Daily Mail, a senior administration official said that U.S. officials are working with the Kenyan government to establish a dedicated facility for asymptomatic individuals who are suspected of having come into contact with the disease. The plan is framed as part of a coordinated, multinational response to the rapidly worsening Ebola emergency in central Africa.
\n\nThe official emphasized the long‑standing health partnership between the two nations, noting that decades of collaboration have benefited both American and Kenyan citizens.
"Our joint response to the current Ebola outbreak is a natural extension of our longstanding cooperation," the statement read. The facility, which would be built in Kenya with the assistance of the State Department, the Department of Defense and the Department of Health and Human Services, is expected to start with around 50 beds. If the situation deteriorates, the capacity could be expanded to as many as 250 beds.
The site would be equipped with biocontainment units, field hospital infrastructure and the necessary medical equipment to treat patients who later develop symptoms. \n\nSecretary of State Marco Rubio addressed the matter at a cabinet meeting, declaring that the United States would not permit Ebola to enter the country.
"The number one priority of our foreign policy is to protect the American people. We cannot and will not allow any cases of Ebola into the US," he said, adding that agencies are actively tracking individuals who may have been exposed.
The administration is also coordinating with European partners; earlier plans called for transferring infected patients to facilities in Europe, but recent reports indicate that Kenya will now serve as the primary treatment hub for any American citizens who develop the disease while abroad. \n\nThe outbreak, centered in the Democratic Republic of Congo and now spreading to neighboring Uganda, has already produced more than 1,000 suspected cases and roughly 220 suspected deaths.
The virus was first identified in the city of Bunia in late April, when a health worker presented with fever, hemorrhaging and vomiting and subsequently died. Testing took three weeks, allowing the disease to spread unchecked. Among the expatriate community, one American missionary doctor tested positive and was airlifted to Germany for advanced care, where his condition is reportedly improving. Another American health worker, who remains asymptomatic, is under observation in Prague.
Health officials estimate that up to 5,000 U.S. citizens may be in the DRC, though the exact number in Uganda is unclear. Because Ebola's incubation period can extend up to 21 days, individuals placed in the Kenyan field hospital could be required to remain there for three weeks while they are monitored for any signs of illness.
The Kenyan facility will also serve as a hub for the distribution of personal protective equipment and the implementation of stringent infection‑control measures at checkpoints and health centers throughout the region. The outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola, a rare strain for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment, underscoring the urgency of the multinational containment effort
